title: RFK Jr.’s vaccine injury clinic could damage NIH hospital, board warns
gist: Jack Leslie, chair of the board overseeing the NIH Clinical Center, used a meeting to rebuke Health Secretary RFK Jr. over a ribbon-cutting for his vaccine injury clinic at which patients sat behind "vaccine injured" placards, warning that it presupposes research conclusions and could damage trust in the 70-year-old hospital. CEO Jonathan Green said the clinic is just a new protocol still under review, in an existing vaccine evaluation center, with no new funding or space; the board unanimously endorsed Leslie's statement.

themes.theme: Board chair rebukes Kennedy's clinic event

insights.claim: Jack Leslie, chair of the board overseeing the NIH Clinical Center Research Hospital, departed from the agenda for six minutes to rebuke Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, warning his anti-vaccine activity could tarnish the hospital.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Rare institutional pushback inside HHS that signals growing governance friction at NIH.
insights.locator: At a recent meeting of the board

insights.claim: Leslie objected to a Kennedy ribbon-cutting for his vaccine injury clinic, where people claiming vaccine injuries sat behind placards reading "vaccine injured" alongside high-ranking Trump administration officials.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Shows how political messaging is shaping federal vaccine research.
insights.locator: Leslie took issue with a recent stunt

insights.claim: The board unanimously endorsed Leslie's statement by voice vote after a member moved to support it.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: A formal, unanimous advisory-board stance against the HHS secretary.

insights.claim: The NIH already has a center that studies vaccine injuries, and Kennedy's new clinic comes with no added funding or clinic space; CEO Jonathan Green described it as merely a new individual protocol.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: The clinic is mostly symbolic and has little real effect on research capacity.
insights.locator: In fact, the NIH already has a center

insights.claim: Green said the protocol will run in the clinical center's vaccine evaluation center, which has existed for decades, and that it is still undergoing required scientific and ethical review.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: No research has started yet, so results are far off.

insights.claim: Leslie argues the vaccine-injured placards announce a conclusion the research is meant to test, so findings of harm will be dismissed as Kennedy's bias and findings of none will be called a sham, leaving patients with answers no one trusts.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Politicized framing can make federal vaccine-safety research useless to policymakers whatever it finds.
insights.quote: Those signs announce the conclusion that the research has not yet reached and that the research exists to test.

insights.claim: Leslie warns that if people believe research at the hospital can be steered toward a politically desired answer, the damage to the hospital's trust, built over 70 years, will not stop at vaccines.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Erosion of trust could spread across the NIH research portfolio, including trials sponsors rely on.
insights.quote: If people come to believe that research at this hospital can be steered toward a politically desired answer, the damage will not stop at vaccines.

insights.claim: Leslie said he has no objection to studying vaccine injuries, calling serious reactions rare but real and saying those who believe they were injured should be taken seriously.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: The objection is to process and optics, not to vaccine-safety research.
insights.quote: Serious reactions are rare, but real
